newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German chemical firms look abroad for growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German chemical firms look abroad for growth.

text.p: A turnaround for Germany's chemical companies is on the cards for 1997, despite a two percent fall in turnover in 1996, Juergen Strube, the head of the German chemical industry group VCI said on Thursday.
"Most of our members expect a somewhat more favourable development of the economy for 1997 than in the previous year and corresponding growth," said Strube, who is also chief executive of BASF AG.
Turnover in the German chemical industry fell two percent in 1996 to just under 177 billion marks ($111 billion), while production grew 0.5 percent and producer prices fell 3.5 percent, the VCI said.
"The reasons for this were, on the one hand, the unsatisfactory price situation and, on the other hand, weak demand, especially in Germany," Strube said.
The main engine for growth in the sector would be foreign business, he said.
The strength of the German chemical industry as an exporting power was underlined by a 3.5 percent increase in chemical exports in 1996 to around 104 billion marks.
At the same time, imports accounted for around 61 billion marks worth of turnover and were down one percent.
The VCI said it had examined the balance sheets of 33 German chemical companies and these studies had shown just how important the foreign market was for them.
The three main chemical companies -- BASF AG, Bayer AG and Hoechst AG -- were strongly focused on their international business and as such had seen good returns, Strube said.
"In 1995 the three main domestic companies saw net returns -- the ratio between post-tax earnings and turnover -- of 7.5 percent," he said.
However, net returns from a group of 30 companies with sales of up to 10 billion marks a year and with less emphasis on international business stood at just 2.9 percent.

"The difference in these two figures shows us just how important it is to intensify our focus on the need for deep restructuring and increased emphasis on foreign business in order to secure jobs in Germany," said Strube.
"There will be further consolidation and cooperation in the chemical sector, as well as increased emphasis on specialisation," he said.
The continuing increase in the value of the dollar to the mark was a mixed blessing. The group benefited on the export side, but it also meant that raw materials were more expensive.
A key factor would be whether or not the industry could offset the increase in raw materials with a rise in prices to the customer, something that it was not clear woud happen.

The VCI said that investment in the chemical sector would stay at around 12 billion marks in 1997, while there would be a small drop in the number of jobs in the sector, albeit less of a fall than in previous years.
